note: A sacrifice that lives, and a man crucified who nevertheless lives. Both phrases hold a death and a life together in one subject rather than in sequence. The graph's pairing, on the shape of the two phrases.

'I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me' (Gal 2:20) holds a death and a life in one person, as 'whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it' (Mark 8:35) does. Neither text cites the other and Paul does not quote the saying, so the pairing is the graph's; what is shared is the structure and the words life and live.

'Then Jesus told His disciples ... For whoever wants to save his life will lose it' (Matt 16:24-25). Named as the speaker in Matthew; Mark 8:34 and Luke 9:23 have the same speech without naming him in the verse.

'if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away.' (2Cor 5:17), beside 'I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live' (Gal 2:20). Both describe an ending and a beginning in the same person, and both locate it 'in Christ'. Paul does not connect the two verses.
Said by Paul at Rom 12:1; the letter names him at Rom 1:1.

'Unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life will lose it' (John 12:24-25). John places the figure immediately before the saying and does not join them with a word. The adjacency is the whole of the evidence, which is why this is implied -- but it is the only place in the corpus where the paradox is given a mechanism.
'whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life' (John 12:25). John's version names what is kept.
